summary: This note introduces the history of relations between Germany and the Soviet Union from 1918 to 1941. It says that cooperation ended in 1933 when Adolf Hitler came to power, that economic ties declined early in the Nazi era, and that some diplomatic initiatives continued through the 1930s. It identifies the 1939 Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact and various trade agreements as culminating points, and notes that Soviet policy toward Nazi Germany under Joseph Stalin is highly controversial in discussions of the origins of the Second World War.
one_line: Overview of Germany–Soviet Union relations from 1918 to 1941, from cooperation's end under Hitler to the 1939 Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact.
key_facts: Cooperation between Germany and the Soviet Union ended in 1933, when Adolf Hitler came to power and created Nazi Germany.
The economic relationship between Germany and the Soviet Union dwindled at the beginning of the Nazi era.
Some diplomatic initiatives between Germany and the Soviet Union continued through the 1930s.
The 1930s diplomatic track culminated with the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact of 1939 and various trade agreements.

The note describes the question of Soviet policy under Joseph Stalin towards Nazi Germany as one of the most controversial and ideologically loaded questions concerning the origins of the Second World War.
The period under examination runs from the Nazi seizure of power to the German invasion of the USSR on June 22, 1941.
The German invasion of the USSR took place on June 22, 1941.
